I have been reading with increasing distress a lot of misinformation about net neutrality, so I decided to make this post to present the real truth. A lot of people don't seem to know exactly what "net neutrality" means; they're just responding to some corporate-sponsored dogwhistles about government regulation and such. This post will provide you with the actual facts about net neutrality and why it must be preserved.

But, don't take my word for it. Ask anyone with a degree or a job in computer science if my explanation is at all incorrect. Seriously, fact-check me. I want you to.

WHAT NET NEUTRALITY ISN'T

Net neutrality is not government regulation. It is not something Obama instituted in 2015. It is not micro-managing the Internet. It does not support monopolies or restrict your freedom. These are all lies spread by corporate ISPs to obscure what they really want to do, which is take away the Internet as you know it now and sell it back to you at a much higher price without providing any increase in service or quality.

WHAT NET NEUTRALITY IS

In order to understand exactly what net neutrality is, you need to understand how computer networks operate. What I'm going to describe applies to all computer networks, not just the Internet. Your home computer network, your employer's computer network, and even the cell phone network all utilize net neutrality. It is an inherent part of the network itself. It is akin to the oil that lubricates your car's engine.

So, how do computer networks operate? To start off, realize that data on a network doesn't travel in a continuous stream. It travels in little, separate pieces called packets. When you stream a video on Netflix, the computer data that makes up each frame is divided into packets and transmitted over the Internet's wires to your phone or computer, where they are reassembled into the video itself. This is how all data travels over a network.

A packet of data is structured in a specific way, called a protocol. The "http" that starts every website on the Internet stands for HyperText Transfer Protocol. There are other protocols in use, as well. Each one is designed to perform a specific task as efficiently as possible. The File Transfer Protocol (FTP) is much better at transmitting large files than HTTP, which is itself much better at transmitting web pages than FTP.

One part of every protocol on the network is the address of the packet's destination. This address is just a number which represents a location on the network. There are machines on the Internet called Domain Name Servers (DNS) that translate these numbers into the text that you read at the top of your browser window. The packet, however, only contains the number.

When a packet is transmitted (like the streaming video mentioned above), it travels over the network to a switch. The switch looks at the incoming packet's address and sends it out along a different wire toward its destination. A packet can travel through many such switches in its trip from the original website to your screen. Each switch looks at the address and routes the packet toward its goal.

Here's where net neutrality finally comes in. The switches don't care where the packet came from. They don't care what is on the computer where the packet is headed. They don't care about the contents of the packet. They only care about the location on the network to which the packet is headed. To the switch, it's just a number. The switch, and thus the network itself, is neutral in the way it handles data packets. Each packet is routed on a first-come, first-served basis. One kind of packet does not have priority over another kind of packet.

That is what net neutrality means. It means the network itself is neutral in the way it handles data packets. Every packet is treated exactly the same as every other packet. Because the network is neutral, your data travels as the highest speed possible no matter where it's going. This has enabled the Internet to be a rousing success when it comes to commerce. Anyone can start a business online, and they are as accessible as Amazon and Google. And it's entirely due to the inherent neutrality of the network.

The greedy, corporate ISPs have realized that they could make more money if they removed neutrality from the Internet. They want to build switches and create protocols that DO care about where your packets are headed and what they contain. They want to be able to prioritize certain packets over other packets. That way, they can charge people more money to have their packets moved to the front of the line.

This means that, instead of paying one set monthly fee for your Internet access, you will pay for tiers of access, the way you pay for channel packages of cable TV. You will have a social media fee, a streaming video fee, an online gaming fee, etc. It also means those same ISPs can turn around and charge the content providers for high-speed access to their customers as well. Comcast could charge Netflix more money to allow Comcast customers the bandwidth they need to stream videos, AND they could charge their own customers for that same bandwidth. They would be making money from both sides of the network. Of course, since a site like Netflix would have to pay more money to each ISP, they would have to raise their rates to compensate, and you, the consumer, would be paying even MORE money for what you already have.

Removing net neutrality would also allow the corporate ISPs to deny access to any website they choose, such as Voat. They could continue to stifle competition by, for example, only allowing high speed access to their in-house streaming video service and only providing much slower speeds to Netflix and YouTube. They could funnel their customers' data toward whatever sites they choose, and they would do so in a way that maximizes their own profits.

This isn't the same as a "data cap." A data cap is a limit on the total amount of data (or the maximum speed) you can access. It doesn't make any distinction between websites. Whatever speed you are paying for is the speed at which all your data travels, whether it's e-mails or video or gaming or posts to Voat.

The 2015 Obama FCC decision reclassified ISPs as utilities, similar to the power or water companies, in response to their efforts to remove net neutrality (called SOPA and CIPA at the time). Doing so prevented them from charging different rates for different ways of using data, the same way the power company can't charge you different rates for using lighbulbs versus microwaves. All of your electricity costs the same, and all of your data costs the same under these regulations. This isn't "micro-management." It prevents corporate exploitation of their monopoly power.

Ajit Pai wants to remove this regulation so that the corporate ISPs can remove net neutrality and charge their consumers more money for the same things they already have. They will not spend that money on more infrastructure or bandwidth. They already received $400 billion in taxpayer money back in the 90's, but they didn't increase their infrastructure with it; they just pocketed the money and started demanding more.

Removing net neutrality is a loss for both consumers and content providers. It does not increase freedom or competition; it stifles both. The only people to benefit from removing neutrality from the Internet are the billionaire stockholders of the corporate ISPs. Don't believe anyone who tries to tell you different.

Net neutrality has always been a part of the Internet. It has always been a part of every computer network ever since computers were first networked together.
